Q: Select randomly a few rows of the same Id in the same table (T-SQL) A:

Try this:

DECLARE @t table(Id int, Review char(6))
INSERT @t values
(1,'Text11'),
(1,'Text12'),
(1,'Text13'),
(2,'Text21'),
(3,'Text31'),
(3,'Text32'),
(4,'Text41'),
(5,'Text51'),
(6,'Text61'),
(6,'Text62'),
(6,'Text63')

;WITH CTE AS
(
SELECT
  id, Review,
  row_number() over (partition by id order by newid()) rn, 
  count(*) over (partition by id) cnt
   FROM @t
 )
 SELECT id, Review
 FROM CTE
 WHERE rn <= (cnt / 10) + 1

Result(random):

id  Review
1   Text12
2   Text21
3   Text31
4   Text41
5   Text51
6   Text63

Q: Redis sentinel vs clustering A:

The recommendation, everywhere, is to start with an odd number of instances, not using two or a multiple of two. That was corrected, but let’s correct some other points.

First, to say that Sentinel provides failover without HA is false. When you have failover, you have HA with the additional benefit of application state being replicated. The distinction is that you can have HA in a system without replication (it's HA, but it's not fault-tolerant).

Second, running a sentinel on the same machine as its target Redis instance is not a "bad setup": if you lose your sentinel, or your Redis instance, or the whole machine, the results are the same. That's probably why every example of such configurations shows both running on the same machine.

Q: Correct way to track pressed keystates on focusing a window A:

You claim that GetAsyncKeyState() is not an option, but that is actually the correct solution.

GetKeyboardState() and GetKeyState() report the calling thread's current key state after any WM_KEY... messages have been processed by that thread. So they're reporting only local state, not global state.

GetAsyncKeyState(), on the other hand, tells you the current global key state, not the local state of the calling thread.

It sounds like what you need is a combination of GetAsyncKeyState() and SetKeyboardState() to update the calling thread.

Otherwise, instead of relying on the calling thread's local key state, you might consider using real-time state events from a global keyboard hook via SetWindowsHookEx(), or even Raw Input events from RegisterRawInputDevices() and WM_INPUT.

Q: Is there a rustc equivalent of -Wall -Werror? A:

In addition to what's already been said, you can also add this to Cargo.toml :

[lints.rust]
warnings = "deny"

Q: When is it appropriate to use a semicolon? A:

Like some other modern languages derived from the C syntax, JavaScript syntax was designed to allow you to omit semicolons in almost all situations. I'd say use them always or use them never*. To use them "never" the long and short of it is that every statement goes on a new line and never begin a line with (, [, or `.

However, to use them "never", you should definitely be using a linter such as JavaScript Standard Style or ESLint with its built-in semi rule to disable semicolons and its no-unexpected-multiline rule which will make sure that you avoid the few gotchas such as the following:

a = b + c
(d + e).foo()

The above is interpreted as a = b + c(d + e).foo();. Note that by following the above rule and not beginning a line with (, this situation is prevented.

Another common example is the following:

return
{
     hello: "world"
};

At a glance, one may think this will be interpreted as returning an object, but it is actually interpreted as return;, and the code to define the object after the return statement is unreachable. Again, by following the rule of not beginning a line with {, this is avoided.

  • *Okay, okay, not never, but almost never.

Q: there are two case_when() in code,the conditions are the same. Is the any way to simplify it A:

Best to build a table and use joins. But you still could use case_when() to index into a data.frame:

cases <- data.frame(
  kpi_a = c("A", "B", "C"),
  kpi_b = c(1.1, 1.2, 2)
)

case <- case_when(
  diamonds$color %in% c("E", "I") ~ 1L,
  diamonds$color %in% c("J", "H") ~ 2L,
  .default = 3L
)

diamonds[c("kpi_a", "kpi_b")] <- cases[case, ]

head(diamonds)

#   <dbl> <ord>     <ord> <ord>   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
# 1  0.23 Ideal     E     SI2      61.5    55   326  3.95  3.98  2.43 A       1.1
# 2  0.21 Premium   E     SI1      59.8    61   326  3.89  3.84  2.31 A       1.1
# 3  0.23 Good      E     VS1      56.9    65   327  4.05  4.07  2.31 A       1.1
# 4  0.29 Premium   I     VS2      62.4    58   334  4.2   4.23  2.63 A       1.1
# 5  0.31 Good      J     SI2      63.3    58   335  4.34  4.35  2.75 B       1.2
# 6  0.24 Very Good J     VVS2     62.8    57   336  3.94  3.96  2.48 B       1.2

You could also use a simple vector since color is a factor variable. But you need to do thorough testing before using something like that, since it relies on the order not changing.

case <- c(3L, 1L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 1L, 2L)[diamonds$color]
